page.question: Private home or hotel for a ski week in Aspen?
page.title: Aspen Ski Week: Private Home or Hotel? A Local's Guide by Neighborhood and Group
page.description: Where Aspen's rental homes are, how each neighborhood gets you to the four mountains, what a hotel gives you that a house cannot, and how holiday-week minimums work. Written from Aspen, with a note on Vail, Beaver Creek and Telluride.
page.capsule: Take a hotel for a couple, a first visit or a short stay: you get ski valet, a concierge and a walk to the gondola. Take a private home for a group of six or more, or a week or longer, where bedrooms, a kitchen and a living room matter more than service. In Aspen the neighborhood decides how easy the skiing is, more than the house does.
answer: We live here, so this is the conversation we have most often in November. Aspen is four separate mountains: Aspen Mountain rises straight out of town, Aspen Highlands and Buttermilk are a short ride down the valley, and Snowmass, the largest, is about twenty minutes away with its own village. A free shuttle links all four. Hotels cluster at the foot of Aspen Mountain and at the base of Snowmass, so a hotel guest is rarely more than a short walk from a lift. {{hotel:The Little Nell}} sits at the gondola and is the only ski-in/ski-out hotel in Aspen itself; {{hotel:Hotel Jerome, Auberge Collection|Hotel Jerome}}, {{hotel:The St. Regis Aspen Resort|The St. Regis}} and {{hotel:MOLLIE Aspen|MOLLIE}} are a few blocks away, and {{hotel:Viceroy Snowmass}} is on the slopes at Snowmass.

Homes are spread wider, and that is the trade. A house gives a group its own bedrooms, a kitchen for breakfast before ski school, a hot tub and a living room where three generations can be together without booking a table. What it takes away is the hotel around you: nobody carries your skis, dinner needs a reservation and a ride, and on a snowy morning the distance to the lift is your problem. For two to four people on a four-night trip a hotel is nearly always the better answer. For eight people over a week, a well-placed home usually is, and it is often the better value per bedroom as well. Our atlas lists {{hotels:region=Colorado&experience=Ski}} Colorado ski hotels; Aspen homes are not in the villa feed and are arranged directly.

paras: The mistake we see most is choosing the house first and the location second. A beautiful home on Red Mountain is the right call for a group that wants long evenings in and has a car service on call. It is the wrong call for a family with small children who need to be at ski school by nine. That family belongs at Snowmass, where most of the beginner and intermediate terrain is and where a ski-in/ski-out home is a real thing and not a figure of speech.

Aspen Mountain has no beginner runs at all, which surprises first-time visitors who booked next to the gondola. Beginners ski Buttermilk or Snowmass, and strong skiers who want steeps head to Highlands. Where you stay should follow who is in the group and where they will actually ski.

paras: A home can be staffed to close most of the gap. A private chef for some evenings, a driver, daily housekeeping, grocery stocking before arrival and ski rental delivered and fitted in the living room are all normal requests here. Budget for them when you compare the house with hotel rooms, because the rental rate alone leaves them out.

sections.h2: Holiday weeks, altitude and getting here
paras: Christmas and New Year are the hardest weeks of the year. Homes commonly ask for a minimum of seven to fourteen nights across the two holidays, hotels set their own minimums, and the best of both are held by returning guests. Presidents week in February and the main March school breaks come next, usually with minimums of five to seven nights. January after the first week, and early April, give you the same houses with far more flexibility.

Aspen sits at about 7,900 feet and Snowmass Village a little higher. Most people feel it on the first day: drink water, go easy on alcohol the first evening and do not plan your hardest ski day first. Aspen's airport, ASE, is ten minutes from town, which is a luxury few ski towns have, but it closes to weather more often than a large airport does. Build in a backup: Eagle is about ninety minutes away by road and Denver about four hours in good conditions.

The same logic travels. In Vail and Beaver Creek, hotels and homes in the villages are walkable to lifts, while gated enclaves such as Bachelor Gulch offer ski-in/ski-out houses with a resort's services nearby. In Telluride the choice is between the old town and Mountain Village, linked by a free gondola. The villa atlas holds {{villas:destination=Colorado}} {{page:/atlas/villa|Colorado homes}}, in Steamboat Springs, Breckenridge, Beaver Creek, Telluride and Vail.

faqs.q: Do I need a car in Aspen?
faqs.a: Not if you stay in the core, the West End or at Snowmass Village. The town is walkable, the four-mountain shuttle is free and hotels run their own cars. On Red Mountain, in Starwood or anywhere up a hill, you need a rental with winter tires or a driver.

faqs.q: Is a private home cheaper than a hotel in Aspen?
faqs.a: Per bedroom, often yes for groups of six or more over a week. In total, not always, once you add a chef, a driver, housekeeping and the cleaning fee and taxes. Compare the full cost of the week, not the nightly rate.

faqs.q: Can a home in Aspen be ski-in/ski-out?
faqs.a: Very few are on Aspen Mountain itself. If skiing from the door matters, look at Snowmass, where many homes and condominiums sit on the runs, or at a slopeside hotel such as The Little Nell in Aspen.

page.question: St. Barts: villa or hotel?
page.title: St. Barts: Villa or Hotel? How the Island Works, Area by Area
page.description: St. Barts is a villa island first, with a handful of small hotels on its best beaches. Which areas suit which stay, why you need a car, what villas include, and how festive-season minimums work, across the {{villas:destination=St. Barthélemy}} St. Barts villas in our atlas.
page.capsule: St. Barts is a villa island. There are no large resorts, the hotels are small and mostly sit on a few beaches, and most of the island's best views belong to hillside homes. Choose a hotel for a short stay, a first visit or if you want the beach at your door. Choose a villa for a week, a group, or privacy, and rent a car either way.
answer: The island is small, steep and almost entirely residential, and that shapes everything. St. Barts never built big resorts. Its hotels are small, most with a few dozen rooms, and they occupy a handful of beaches: {{hotel:Eden Rock - St Barths, Oetker Hotels|Eden Rock}} on St. Jean, {{hotel:Cheval Blanc St-Barth}} on Flamands, {{hotel:Le Sereno}} and {{hotel:Le Barthelemy Hotel & Spa|Le Barthélemy}} on the lagoon at Grand Cul de Sac. The rest of the island's accommodation is private villas on the hillsides, which is why the villa side of our atlas is so much deeper here: {{villas:destination=St. Barthélemy}} {{page:/atlas/villa|St. Barts villas}} against {{hotels:country=Saint Barthélemy}} {{page:/hotels/saint-barthelemy|hotels}}.

The honest difference is beach against view. A hotel puts you on the sand with a restaurant, a bar and people to look after you. A villa usually puts you up a hill with a pool, a terrace and a view over the water, and a ten-minute drive to whichever beach you feel like that day. Neither is the lesser choice. St. Barts is an island where you go out, to a different beach in the morning and a different restaurant at night, and a villa suits that rhythm well. For a stay of three or four nights, or a first visit when you do not yet know the island, a hotel is simpler.

paras: Villas on St. Barts are closer to a serviced stay than a rental house elsewhere. Housekeeping normally comes daily except Sundays and holidays, someone meets you at the airport and leads you to the house, and a local concierge can stock the kitchen and book restaurants before you land. What a villa does not have is a front desk at midnight or a beach attendant, and that is the real gap to weigh.

sections.h2: Which part of the island
list: Gustavia: the harbor town, with the shops and many of the restaurants. Villas here and on the hill above trade a beach for walking to dinner. Shell Beach is on foot.
St. Jean: the most convenient base. A long swimming beach, beach clubs, shops and the airport all close together. Busy by island standards.
Flamands: the widest beach on the island and a quiet residential feel, at the far western end of the road.
Lorient: a local, low-key village with a good family beach and a surf break. Central for driving anywhere.
Pointe Milou: a rocky point of cliffside villas facing the sunset. No beach of its own, but the views are the reason people return to the same house.
Gouverneur and Lurin: hillside estates above one of the island's most beautiful undeveloped beaches. Private and quiet, with a steep road.
Grand Cul de Sac: a shallow, calm lagoon suited to children, paddleboards and kites, with several of the hotels.
Toiny and Grand Fond: the wild, windward coast. Dramatic and peaceful, but the sea here is not for casual swimming.
paras: You need a car almost wherever you stay. The roads are narrow, steep and short, nothing is more than twenty minutes away, and taxis are few. Small cars and open-top runabouts are the island norm, and your villa manager or hotel will have one waiting at the airport.

sections.h2: Seasons, festive weeks and getting there
paras: The season runs from mid-December to April. Christmas and New Year are in a category of their own: villas commonly ask for minimum stays of ten to fourteen nights, hotels set their own minimums, and the best houses are taken by the same families year after year. If you want those weeks, start a year ahead. January after the first week, March and April are easier, and May through July is quieter and warmer with the island still open. Many hotels and restaurants close from late August into October, the peak of hurricane season.

There are no long-haul flights. The runway is short, so most travelers fly to St. Maarten and connect by a small plane, a flight of about fifteen minutes with a famous approach over the hill, or by a ferry that takes under an hour. There are also small-plane services from San Juan. Allow for the connection when you choose flights, and avoid a tight same-day link on the way home.

faqs.q: Are there villas on the beach in St. Barts?
faqs.a: A few, mainly on Flamands, Lorient, St. Jean and the lagoon at Grand Cul de Sac, and they book early. Most villas are on the hillsides, a short drive from the sand. If walking onto a beach matters more than a view, a beachfront hotel is the surer choice.

faqs.q: Is St. Barts good for families with children?
faqs.a: Yes, particularly in a villa. A private pool, separate bedrooms and a kitchen make the days easy, and Grand Cul de Sac, Lorient and St. Jean have calm water. Check pool fencing and stairs with small children, as many villas are built into slopes.

faqs.q: How many nights do you need in St. Barts?
faqs.a: Five to seven nights suits most visitors. The connection through St. Maarten or San Juan takes part of a day each way, and the pleasure of the island is trying a different beach and restaurant each day.

page.question: Caribbean by luxury yacht: which islands, and when?
page.title: The Caribbean by Luxury Yacht: Which Islands, Which Route and When to Go
page.description: What a yacht-sized ship reaches in the Caribbean that a large ship does not, northern against southern routes, where you board, and the December to April season, across the {{journeys:collection=yacht&region=CARIB}} Caribbean yacht itineraries in our atlas.
page.capsule: A yacht-sized ship reaches the small Caribbean: Gustavia in St. Barts, Jost Van Dyke and Virgin Gorda, Bequia and the Grenadines, English Harbour in Antigua. Choose a northern route for St. Barts and the Virgin Islands, a southern one for the Grenadines and St. Lucia. Sail between mid-December and April, when the weather is dry and the yachts are here.
answer: Large cruise ships in the Caribbean go where there are piers long enough to take them: St. Thomas, Philipsburg, Bridgetown, Nassau. The islands most people picture when they think of the Caribbean are somewhere else, in bays with a few dozen boats at anchor and a beach bar on the sand. Yacht-style ships are built for those places. They anchor off Gustavia, Jost Van Dyke or Bequia, put guests ashore by tender in a few minutes, and often stay into the evening when the day visitors have gone. On a calm day they open a marina at the waterline, and you swim from the ship.

Our atlas holds {{journeys:collection=yacht&region=CARIB}} {{page:/journeys/yacht|Caribbean yacht itineraries}}: {{journeys:operator=Four Seasons Yachts&region=CARIB}} from {{op:yacht/Four Seasons Yachts|Four Seasons}}, {{journeys:operator=Orient Express Sailing Yachts&region=CARIB}} from {{op:yacht/Orient Express Sailing Yachts|Orient Express}}, {{journeys:operator=Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection&region=CARIB}} from {{op:yacht/Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection|Ritz-Carlton}} and {{journeys:operator=Aman at Sea&region=CARIB}} from {{op:yacht/Aman at Sea|Aman at Sea}}, whose first ship does not enter service until 2027. Most are seven to ten nights. The choice that matters more than the brand is the route, because the northern and southern Caribbean are quite different trips.

The yacht's size shows most at the smallest stops. Gustavia's harbor is full of private yachts and has no pier for ships, so every ship anchors outside; a small one has its guests ashore in minutes and can stay late. Jost Van Dyke, Bequia and the Tobago Cays work the same way. At English Harbour in Antigua, the Georgian dockyard was built for sailing ships and still feels that scale.

paras: The yacht lines follow the sun. They spend the winter here and cross the Atlantic in spring for the Mediterranean summer, then return in late autumn. That makes the Caribbean season short and fixed, and the festive weeks in particular sell early.

Most itineraries begin or end in San Juan, St. Maarten, Bridgetown in Barbados, or Fort Lauderdale and Miami, with some using Antigua or St. Lucia. San Juan and the Florida ports are the easiest to reach from the United States. Barbados is the natural gateway for the Grenadines. Whichever it is, arrive the day before: ships sail on time, and winter weather at home delays flights more often than anything in the Caribbean does.

faqs.q: Is the Caribbean rough on a small ship?
faqs.a: Mostly not. Passages between neighboring islands are short and often overnight. The open channels between islands can be lively when the trade winds are strong, most often in December and January, and the southern route has longer passages than the northern one.

faqs.q: Can you swim from the ship?
faqs.a: On the yacht-style ships, usually yes, when the ship is at anchor and the sea is calm. A platform or marina opens at the waterline with paddleboards and kayaks. It depends on conditions and local rules, so treat it as likely but not promised at any given stop.

faqs.q: Is a yacht cruise better than a villa or resort in the Caribbean?
faqs.a: It is a different trip. A yacht shows you five or six islands with no packing and no flights between them. A villa or resort gives you one island properly. Many travelers combine them, with a few nights ashore before or after the sailing.

page.question: The Drake Passage: should you sail it or fly over it?
page.title: The Drake Passage: Sail It or Fly Over It? An Honest Comparison
page.description: What two days across the Drake Passage are really like, what a fly-cruise from Punta Arenas saves and risks, and who should choose each, including the fly-one-way option, across the {{journeys:collection=cruise&region=Antarctica}} Antarctic voyages in our atlas.
page.capsule: Sail the Drake Passage if you have the time and can tolerate the chance of two rough days each way: you get more ship choice, lower cost and the sense of arriving. Fly over it if you are short of time or badly prone to seasickness, accepting higher cost, fewer ships and the chance of a weather delay. Flying one way is a good compromise.
answer: The Drake Passage is the roughly 600 miles of open ocean between the tip of South America and the Antarctic Peninsula. Ships leaving Ushuaia take about two days to cross it in each direction. Nobody can tell you in advance what you will get. Some crossings are flat calm, which crews call the Drake Lake, and some bring heavy swell for a day or more. Most are somewhere in between: a noticeable roll, a quiet dining room on the first evening, and people finding their feet by the second day. Modern expedition ships have stabilizers and captains time the crossing around the weather, which helps a great deal but does not remove the motion.

The alternative is to fly. A fly-cruise takes a charter flight of about two hours from Punta Arenas in Chile to an airstrip on King George Island in the South Shetlands, where the ship is waiting. You are in Antarctica the same day and you skip four days at sea. The cost is real, though: the fare is higher, far fewer ships offer it, and the flight needs clear weather at a gravel runway with no instrument landing, so delays of a day or more happen. Of the {{journeys:collection=cruise&region=Antarctica}} {{page:/journeys/cruise|Antarctic voyages}} in our atlas, most sail both ways.

paras: Antarctica21 pioneered the fly-cruise, and Quark Expeditions, Aurora Expeditions, Silversea and Lindblad are among the operators that now offer flights on some departures. The ships used are often at the smaller end, which is a point in their favor once you arrive, since landings are limited to a hundred people ashore at a time.

Ask how an operator handles a delayed flight before you book. The good ones have a written contingency plan: a set window in which they will keep trying to fly, activities in Punta Arenas while you wait, and a stated refund if the flight cannot operate at all. Luggage limits on the charter aircraft are also stricter than on a ship. Leave buffer days in Chile at the end of the trip, and do not book a tight connection home.

sections.h2: What you gain by sailing
paras: The crossing is part of the expedition, not dead time. Albatrosses and petrels follow the ship for hours. The expedition team uses the sea days for lectures on ice, wildlife and the history of the place, and for the briefings and boot fittings that would otherwise eat into your time on the Peninsula. Somewhere on the second day the air turns cold, the first iceberg appears, and you understand how far you have come. People who fly arrive in Antarctica rested. People who sail arrive feeling that they have earned it, and many say the return crossing, with the photographs sorted and new friends made, is one of the pleasures of the trip.
list: Speak to your doctor before you travel about a prescription patch or tablets, and start them before the ship leaves sheltered water, not once you feel ill.
Choose a cabin low and near the middle of the ship, where motion is least. This matters more on the Drake than a balcony does.
A larger, stabilized ship rides more comfortably than a very small one, at the price of slower landings. It is a real trade-off.
Eat lightly, stay hydrated, get air on deck and look at the horizon. Most people are fine by the second day.
Longer voyages that include South Georgia and the Falklands spread the sea days out and are always sailed, never flown.

faqs.q: How bad is the Drake Passage, really?
faqs.a: It varies from calm to very rough and cannot be predicted when you book. A typical crossing has a steady roll that many guests feel on the first day and adapt to by the second. Severe crossings happen but are the minority, and captains adjust speed and timing to avoid the worst weather.

faqs.q: Is flying to Antarctica safer or more reliable than sailing?
faqs.a: Neither is unsafe. Sailing is the more reliable of the two for schedule: ships cross in almost any weather. Flights depend on visibility and wind at King George Island and are sometimes delayed by a day or more, occasionally longer.

faqs.q: Can you avoid the Drake Passage completely?
faqs.a: Yes, by flying both ways, or by choosing a different trip such as the Ross Sea from New Zealand, which has its own long ocean passage. For the Antarctic Peninsula, the only alternative to the Drake by sea is the flight.

page.question: Seabourn, Silversea, Regent or Crystal: which ultra-luxury cruise line suits you?
page.title: Seabourn vs Silversea vs Regent vs Crystal: Which Ultra-Luxury Cruise Line Suits You
page.description: The four classic ultra-luxury cruise lines compared on ship size, what the fare includes, suites and butlers, dining, atmosphere and where each is strongest, with an honest note on who each does not suit.
page.capsule: Choose Regent if you want nearly everything in the fare, shore excursions included. Choose Silversea for the widest choice of destinations and a butler in every suite. Choose Seabourn for a relaxed, sociable ship that feels like a private club. Choose Crystal for classic big-ship cruising with the most space, entertainment and dining variety. All four include drinks and gratuities.
answer: These four lines sit in the same tier and compete for the same travelers, so the differences are of emphasis, not of quality. All four sail all-suite or nearly all-suite ships of a few hundred guests, include drinks and gratuities in the fare, and staff their ships at close to one crew member for every guest and a half. What separates them is how much else the fare covers, how formal the evenings are, and what kind of company you will keep. Regent is the most inclusive and the most popular with North Americans who like a full day of touring. Silversea is the most international and goes to the most places. Seabourn is the most relaxed. Crystal is the most traditional.

In our atlas, {{op:cruise/Seabourn}} has {{journeys:operator=Seabourn}} itineraries and {{op:cruise/Silversea}} {{journeys:operator=Silversea}}, many of them expedition voyages. {{op:worldcruise/Regent Seven Seas|Regent}} ({{journeys:operator=Regent Seven Seas}}) and {{op:worldcruise/Crystal}} ({{journeys:operator=Crystal}}) appear through their world cruises and the segments of them, which are a good way to try either line for three or four weeks. Fares between the four are closer than the brochures suggest once you add back what one line includes and another does not, so compare the total cost of the trip: flights, excursions, a hotel night before, and Wi-Fi.

If you prefer to walk off the ship and wander, or to hire a private guide, you are paying for something you will not use, and Seabourn or Silversea's cruise-only fare may serve you better.

sections.h2: Who each line does not suit
list: Seabourn: not for travelers who want a butler, a wide choice of evening shows, or excursions bundled in. The pleasure is the ship's easy social life, the open bars and the service that learns your name on the first day.

Silversea: not for those who want a lively ship. Evenings are quiet and the guests are a mix of nationalities who largely keep their own company. Its newest ships are the largest of the four lines' classic fleets, and its older ones the smallest, so the ship matters.
Regent: not for the independent traveler, since so much of the fare is touring. The ships are among the most spacious at sea, and evenings are early because days ashore are full.

Crystal: not for anyone seeking a small-ship feel or small harbors. Its two ships are larger and older in design, rebuilt with far fewer guests than they once carried. In return you get the most choice of restaurants, lectures, classes and music, which is why world cruisers are loyal to it.
paras: A useful first question is how you spend a day in port. If the answer is a guided tour, start with Regent. If it is a long lunch you found yourself, start with Seabourn or Silversea. If the days at sea are what you are looking forward to, start with Crystal. Booking through an advisor matters here mainly because the consortium amenities on these lines, shipboard credit and hosted events, are worth having and cost nothing extra.

sections.h2: Suites, dining and dress
paras: All four are suites with ocean views, and almost all have balconies. Regent's entry suites are generally the largest, and its top suites are the most extravagant at sea. Silversea's newest ships have unusually open, light public spaces and a strong regional food program. Seabourn's ships have the feel of a large private yacht, with a marina that opens at the stern on calm days. Crystal's suites were enlarged when the ships were rebuilt, by combining older cabins.

Dining is open-seating on all four, with several specialty restaurants and room service course by course. Dress is elegant casual most nights across the board. Seabourn and Silversea keep a formal-optional evening on longer voyages, Crystal holds on to the most tradition, and Regent is the least formal.

faqs.q: Which ultra-luxury cruise line is the most all-inclusive?
faqs.a: Regent Seven Seas. Its fare includes shore excursions in every port as well as drinks, gratuities and specialty dining, and on its all-inclusive fare, flights in many markets. Silversea comes closest on its door-to-door fare. Seabourn and Crystal include drinks, gratuities and dining but charge for excursions and flights.

faqs.q: Which line is best for a first luxury cruise?
faqs.a: Seabourn or Regent for most people. Seabourn is the easiest to feel at home on, and Regent removes almost every decision about what to pay for. Choose Silversea first if the destination is the point, since it sails to more places than the others.

faqs.q: Do these lines suit solo travelers?
faqs.a: Yes, better than most. Open seating, hosted tables and included drinks make it easy to meet people, especially on Seabourn and Crystal. Solo supplements vary widely by sailing, and reduced-supplement departures are worth asking about.

page.question: Which Paris palace hotel should you book?
page.title: Which Paris Palace Hotel Should You Book? The Official Palaces Compared by Neighborhood
page.description: What the official Palace distinction means, the thirteen Paris hotels that hold it after the 2026 review, and how to choose between them by neighborhood, character, pool and who is traveling, with the {{hotels:city=Paris}} Paris hotels in our atlas.
page.capsule: Palace is an official French distinction above five stars, and thirteen Paris hotels hold it. For a first visit, choose Le Meurice or the Crillon for the Tuileries and the Louvre on foot. For grand tradition and service, the George V or Le Bristol. For shopping, Plaza Athénée. For a quieter, residential stay, La Réserve or Lutetia on the Left Bank.
answer: In France, Palace is not a marketing word. It is a distinction awarded by the state tourism agency to five-star hotels judged exceptional for their history, setting, service and character, and it is reviewed every few years. After the review announced in June 2026, thirteen hotels in Paris hold it: {{hotel:Le Bristol Paris, Oetker Hotels|Le Bristol}}, {{hotel:Four Seasons Hotel George V}}, Le Meurice, Plaza Athénée, {{hotel:Hotel de Crillon, A Rosewood Hotel|Hôtel de Crillon}}, {{hotel:Le Royal Monceau - Raffles Paris|Le Royal Monceau}}, {{hotel:Shangri-La Paris}}, {{hotel:La Reserve Paris Hotel and Spa|La Réserve}}, {{hotel:The Peninsula Paris}}, {{hotel:Mandarin Oriental Lutetia Paris|Lutetia}}, and three added in 2026, {{hotel:Bvlgari Hotel Paris}}, {{hotel:Cheval Blanc Paris}} and {{hotel:Fouquet's Paris}}.

The list is a useful shortlist, not a ranking, and it is not the whole of the top tier. The {{hotel:Ritz Paris}} on Place Vendôme does not hold the distinction and is a palace in every ordinary sense of the word. The {{hotel:Park Hyatt Paris-Vendome|Park Hyatt Paris-Vendôme}} and the {{hotel:Mandarin Oriental, Paris|Mandarin Oriental on Rue Saint-Honoré}} left the list in 2026 and remain excellent hotels. So choose by where you want to wake up and what kind of hotel you like, then check the label. Our atlas holds {{hotels:city=Paris}} {{page:/hotels/france|Paris hotels}}, and at this level the benefits an advisor adds, breakfast, a credit and an upgrade when available, are worth having on every one of them.

page.question: How far ahead do you need to book a villa for Christmas, New Year and peak summer?
page.title: How Far Ahead to Book a Villa for Christmas, New Year and Peak Summer: A Booking Calendar
page.description: A booking calendar for the weeks when villas sell out: festive weeks in the Caribbean and the ski towns, February and March school breaks, and July and August in Italy, France, Greece and Spain, with minimum stays and the shoulder weeks that give the same house for less.
page.capsule: For Christmas and New Year in the Caribbean or a ski town, book nine to twelve months ahead, and expect minimum stays of seven to fourteen nights. For July and August in Europe, book by the previous autumn or winter. February and March school breaks need six to nine months. Shoulder weeks can be booked a few months out and cost noticeably less.
answer: The best villas are single objects. A hotel has two hundred rooms and can always find another one; a six-bedroom house on the beach in Turks and Caicos has exactly one Christmas week a year. That is why the peak weeks behave differently from the rest of the calendar. The largest and best-placed homes are usually offered first to the family who had them the year before, often before that family has left, and only what they release reaches the market. By the time most people start thinking about next Christmas, in late summer, the choice among large homes in St. Barts, Barbados or Aspen is already thin.

The lead time depends on three things: how fixed your dates are, how many bedrooms you need, and how particular you are about location. A couple who can travel in the second week of January has months to decide. A family of twelve that needs December 26 to January 2, on a swimming beach, needs to start nearly a year out. The villa atlas holds {{collection:villa}} {{page:/atlas/villa|homes}}, and for any of them the calendar below is the realistic guide. An advisor is most useful at the two ends: early, to get onto the list for a specific house, and late, to know which good homes have just come back after a cancellation.

paras: Festive weeks carry their own rules as well as their own prices. Many owners sell Christmas and New Year only as one block of ten to fourteen nights. Others split it into a Christmas week and a New Year week, with New Year the more expensive of the two. Payment and cancellation terms are usually stricter than at other times of year, with a larger deposit and an earlier final payment, so read them before you commit and insure the trip.

In Europe the pressure comes from the school calendar. August is when much of the continent takes its own holiday, so Italian, French and Spanish families are competing for the same houses. High summer rentals are commonly sold Saturday to Saturday, which also fixes your flight days.

sections.h2: What is realistic if you are late
list: Be flexible on dates before you are flexible on quality. Arriving on December 19 and leaving on the 27th, or starting January 2, opens homes that are closed to a December 26 arrival.
Drop a bedroom requirement if you can. Four- and five-bedroom homes are far more numerous than seven-bedroom ones, and two neighboring villas sometimes solve a large group.
Look one island over. When St. Barts is full, Anguilla and St. Martin may not be. When Barbados is full, look at Antigua or Jamaica.
Ask about cancellations. Peak weeks do come back, typically around the date final payment falls due, a few months before arrival.
Consider a resort residence or a hotel villa. They hold more inventory, and you gain the hotel's services.
Do not expect a discount. A late peak week is priced like an early one, and what remains is often what others passed over.

sections.h2: The shoulder weeks that give the same house for less
paras: If your dates can move, move them. In the Caribbean, the first three weeks of December, the stretch from the second week of January to early February, and late April into May offer the same villas and the same weather at a fraction of the festive rate, with short minimum stays. In the ski towns, January after New Year week and late March are the equivalents, and January often has the best snow.

In Europe, June and September are the weeks to aim for. The sea is warm in September, the heat has eased, restaurants are open and unhurried, and a house that insists on seven nights in August may take four or five. May and October work well in Sicily, Puglia and Greece, with cooler evenings and pools that may be too cold unless heated. Late summer and autumn in the Caribbean is hurricane season, when rates are lowest and some homes close; it can be a good trip with the right insurance and the right island.

faqs.q: When should I book a Caribbean villa for Christmas?
faqs.a: Between January and March of the same year for the widest choice of larger homes, and no later than early summer. The best beachfront houses are often rebooked by the same guests a year ahead, so if you have a particular villa in mind, ask to be told the moment it becomes available.

faqs.q: Why do villas have minimum stays at the holidays?
faqs.a: Because an owner who sells four nights in the middle of the festive period cannot sell the nights either side of them. A seven- to fourteen-night minimum protects the most valuable two weeks of the year. Outside those weeks, minimums drop to three to five nights.

faqs.q: Is it cheaper to book a villa at the last minute?
faqs.a: Sometimes in shoulder and low season, when an owner would sooner fill an empty week. Almost never in peak weeks, when demand exceeds supply and what is left late is rarely the house you wanted.

page.question: Where should you rent a villa in Italy: Tuscany, the Amalfi Coast, Puglia, Sicily or the lakes?
page.title: Where to Rent a Villa in Italy: Tuscany, Amalfi Coast, Puglia, Sicily and the Lakes Compared
page.description: Italy's five main villa regions compared: what the houses are like, whether you need a car, pool season and summer heat, and who each suits, across the {{villas:destination=Italy}} Italian villas in our atlas.
page.capsule: Rent in Tuscany for a first villa trip, a big family and day trips to Florence and Siena. Choose the Amalfi Coast for couples and views, accepting stairs and crowds. Choose Puglia for space, beaches and value, Sicily for a longer season and more to explore, and the lakes for cooler weather, boats and an easy arrival through Milan.
answer: An Italian villa holiday is really five different holidays, and the region decides which one you get. Tuscany is the countryside one: a stone farmhouse among vines and cypresses, a pool, long lunches and hill towns within an hour. The Amalfi Coast is vertical and dramatic, with terraces above the sea and a boat for the day. Puglia is flat, bright and relaxed, with whitewashed farm estates and beaches on two coasts. Sicily is the largest and most varied, part beach, part baroque towns, part volcano. The lakes are the elegant northern option, with gardens to the water and the Alps behind. The villa atlas holds {{villas:destination=Italy}} {{page:/atlas/villa|Italian homes}}, {{villas:destination=Italy&location=Tuscany}} of them in Tuscany, {{villas:destination=Italy&location=Amalfi Coast}} on the Amalfi Coast and {{villas:destination=Italy&location=Sicily}} in Sicily, with smaller lists for the lakes and Puglia.

Three practical questions narrow it quickly. Do you want to drive? Tuscany, Puglia and Sicily need a car, the Amalfi Coast is better without one, and the lakes work either way. How hot can you bear it? July and August are very hot everywhere south of Florence, which makes a pool and air conditioning matters to check, not assume. And who is coming? Large family groups do best in Tuscany and Puglia, where big houses with grounds are common. Couples and small groups get more from Amalfi and the lakes, where the setting is the point and the houses are smaller.

paras: Tuscany is the safest first choice because it forgives everything. The houses are large and well set up for rental, the drives are short and beautiful, and a rainy day has Florence, Siena or Lucca within reach. Its weakness is that it is inland, so there is no beach, and in August it is hot and busy.

The Amalfi Coast is the most beautiful and the least convenient. Many villas sit well above or below the road and are reached by long flights of steps, luggage is carried by porters, few houses have parking and fewer have a large pool. Go for the view from the terrace and days on the water, and take a hotel instead if anyone in the group has trouble with stairs.

sections.h2: Puglia, Sicily and the lakes in more detail
paras: Puglia, the heel of the boot, has become the alternative to Tuscany for families. A masseria gives you a walled estate with a pool among olive trees, and the towns of the Itria Valley, Ostuni, Locorotondo, Alberobello, are close together. Beaches are a short drive on either the Adriatic or the Ionian side. It is more casual and generally better value than Tuscany, and the food is some of the best in the country. Fly into Bari or Brindisi.

Sicily rewards a longer stay. The southeast, around Noto, Ragusa and Modica, has the baroque towns and many of the best villas; the east has Taormina and Etna; the west has Palermo, salt flats and Greek temples. Distances are greater than they look, so choose one corner. The season is the longest in Italy, with swimming from May well into October. Fly into Catania or Palermo.

The lakes are the choice for people who do not want heat or a hire car. Como has the grand lakefront villas and the easiest access, about an hour from Milan. Days are spent on boats, in gardens and in the villages of the central lake. Villas here are fewer and command a premium, and a lake is for looking at and boating on more than for swimming.
list: Pools: the season runs from about May to September, and many pools are unheated. Ask, if you are traveling at either end.
Air conditioning: common in newer and renovated villas, not universal in old farmhouses with thick walls. Ask, for July and August.
Changeover day: in high summer most villas rent Saturday to Saturday for a minimum of seven nights.
Staff: a cook for some evenings, daily housekeeping and a driver for winery days can be arranged almost everywhere and change the holiday.
Size of group: sleeping twelve or more in one house is easiest in Tuscany and Puglia.

faqs.q: Which part of Italy is best for a first villa holiday?
faqs.a: Tuscany. The villas are the most numerous and the best equipped for rental, there is something to do within an hour in every direction, and it suits groups of mixed ages. Choose the area between Florence and Siena, or the Val d'Orcia to the south, and avoid August if you can.

faqs.q: Do I need a car for an Italian villa?
faqs.a: In Tuscany, Puglia and Sicily, yes, and for a large group two smaller cars are easier than one van on narrow roads. On the Amalfi Coast a car is a burden, so use a driver and boats. On the lakes you can manage with ferries, water taxis and the occasional driver.

faqs.q: When is the best time to rent a villa in Italy?
faqs.a: June and September. The weather is warm enough for the pool, the heat and crowds of July and August are absent, and prices and minimum stays are lower. May and early October are lovely for touring but can be too cool for unheated pools.

page.capsule: Four Seasons Yachts is the hotel company's move to sea: a 95-suite yacht, Four Seasons I, with a second to follow. Expect very large suites, a marina that opens onto the water and hotel-style service. It is priced like a Four Seasons resort, not an all-inclusive cruise, so dinners and drinks are extra. The product is new, with a short track record.
answer: Four Seasons I entered service in March 2026, and it is best understood as a floating Four Seasons resort and not as a cruise ship. It carries 95 suites and no ordinary cabins, on a hull that most lines would fill with two or three times as many. Suites have floor-to-ceiling glass and terraces, many can be joined into larger residences for a family, and the largest occupy several decks. There is a long pool on the aft deck, a marina that opens on both sides at the waterline for swimming and water sports, a spa, and a range of restaurants and bars more typical of a resort than of a ship this size. A second yacht, Four Seasons II, follows.

Our atlas holds {{journeys:operator=Four Seasons Yachts}} {{op:yacht/Four Seasons Yachts|Four Seasons Yachts}} itineraries with {{departures:operator=Four Seasons Yachts}} departures: {{journeys:operator=Four Seasons Yachts&region=MED}} in the western Mediterranean, {{journeys:operator=Four Seasons Yachts&region=ADRIATIC}} in the Adriatic, {{journeys:operator=Four Seasons Yachts&region=AEGEAN}} in the Aegean and {{journeys:operator=Four Seasons Yachts&region=CARIB}} in the Caribbean. The pattern is the Mediterranean from spring to autumn and the Caribbean in winter. Voyages can usually be joined together, so a week can become two without repeating a port.

paras: The way the fare works is the thing to understand before you compare prices. Most luxury cruise lines sell an inclusive fare, and guests rarely see a bill. Four Seasons has chosen the resort model, where the rate buys the suite and the rest is ordered from a menu. For some travelers that is the appeal: you pay for the dinners and wines you choose, and nobody else's. For others it comes as a surprise on the last morning. Ask for the current list of what is included on your sailing and budget for the rest as you would at a resort.

It is also a new product. The first season has been well received, the hardware is exceptional, and the company knows service. But there are few past guests to learn from yet, itineraries are still being refined, and the second ship is not in the water. If you want a proven routine, the established yacht-style lines have years behind them. If being early appeals, this is the most ambitious new ship at sea.

page.question: When is the best time to go on safari, country by country?
page.title: The Best Time to Go on Safari, Country by Country and Month by Month
page.description: A month-by-month safari calendar for Kenya, Tanzania, Botswana, South Africa, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Namibia, Rwanda and Uganda: dry season against green season, the Okavango flood, and where to go when your dates are fixed.
page.capsule: For most of Africa the best safari months are the dry season, June to October, when animals gather at water and the bush is thin. East Africa has a second good window from late December to February. Botswana's Okavango is at its best from June to September, when the flood is in. The green season costs less, with fewer vehicles and more rain.
answer: Safari timing comes down to water. In the dry season the grass dies back, the leaves fall and animals have to come to the rivers and waterholes that remain, so they are easy to find and easy to see. In the rains the bush turns green and thick, water is everywhere and the animals spread out. Southern Africa, from Botswana and Zambia down to South Africa, has one dry season, roughly May to October. East Africa, Kenya and northern Tanzania, has two: the long dry season from late June to October and a shorter one from late December to February, with the heaviest rain in April and May and lighter rain in November.

Dry is not the same as better for everyone. The green season has newborn animals, migrant birds, dramatic skies and lodges at their lowest rates of the year with few other vehicles about. Photographers and repeat visitors often prefer it. What it risks is an afternoon lost to rain, some roads and camps closed, and game that takes more finding. Our atlas holds {{journeys:collection=safari&country=Botswana}} safari itineraries in Botswana, {{journeys:collection=safari&country=Kenya}} in Kenya, {{journeys:collection=safari&country=South Africa}} in South Africa, {{journeys:collection=safari&country=Tanzania}} in Tanzania and {{journeys:collection=safari&country=Rwanda}} in Rwanda, among {{collection:safari}} {{page:/journeys/safari|in all}}.

sections.h2: The calendar: nine countries, twelve months

table.caption: Peak: the best game viewing and the highest rates. Good: reliable. Mixed: can go either way. Green: rains, low rates, lush. Wet: heavy rain, some camps closed. Hot: excellent game, punishing heat. Rains vary from year to year.

paras: A few entries need explaining. Tanzania's February peak is the calving season in the southern Serengeti, from late January to early March, when the wildebeest herds give birth on the short-grass plains and predators follow. Kenya's July to October peak is the migration in the Masai Mara. Those are covered month by month in {{page:/answers/best-time-to-see-the-great-migration-month-by-month|our migration calendar}}.

Botswana runs on a different clock from its rain. The Okavango Delta floods with water that fell months earlier in Angola, arriving around May or June, standing highest in July and August and receding by October. So the Delta is at its wettest in the middle of the dry season, which is why June to September is so sought after and so expensive. {{page:/answers/okavango-delta-water-camp-vs-land-camp|Water camps and land camps}} experience it differently.

October is the month of extremes in Botswana, Zambia and Zimbabwe: the game viewing is at its most concentrated and the heat is severe. Zambia's South Luangwa is a true seasonal park, and many of its bush camps close from about November to May.

sections.h2: If your dates are fixed
list: July and August, school holidays: everything is at its best and its busiest. Book nine to twelve months ahead. Botswana and Zambia for exclusivity, Kenya or Tanzania for the migration, South Africa for younger children.
Christmas and New Year: East Africa is in its short dry season and works well. South Africa is green and warm, and pairs with Cape Town at its summer best. Avoid Zambia and much of Zimbabwe.
February: the southern Serengeti for calving, or Kenya. In Botswana and South Africa this is green season, with low rates and good birding.
Easter and April: the hardest month. South Africa is the reliable choice, as the rains end there first. East Africa is at its wettest.
June: a quietly excellent month. Dry season has begun almost everywhere, rates are often still below peak and the crowds have not arrived.
October half-term: superb game in southern Africa if you can take the heat; choose a lodge with a pool and air conditioning.
Thanksgiving week: a gamble on early rain. South Africa and Kenya are the safer picks.
paras: South Africa is the most forgiving country in any month. Its private reserves are smaller and well supplied with water, guides find the animals whatever the season, and several areas are malaria-free: Madikwe, the Eastern Cape reserves, the Waterberg and the Kalahari. That makes them the usual recommendation for families with small children and for anyone who prefers not to take antimalarial medication, a decision to make with a travel doctor.

sections.h2: Gorillas, Namibia and Victoria Falls
paras: Gorilla trekking in Rwanda and Uganda runs all year, and the gorillas do not care about the weather. You will, though: the trails are steep and muddy, so the two drier spells, June to September and December to February, are the comfortable months and the ones in which permits sell out first. Rwanda against Uganda is {{page:/answers/gorilla-trekking-rwanda-vs-uganda|a separate decision}}.

Namibia is a desert destination, so rain matters less than temperature. May to October brings cool, clear days and animals gathered at the waterholes of Etosha. Victoria Falls, shared by Zambia and Zimbabwe, peaks at a different time from the game: the falls are fullest from about March to May, after the rains, and at their lowest by October and November, when the Zambian side can be nearly dry.

faqs.q: What is the single best month for a safari?
faqs.a: August or September across most of Africa. It is dry season everywhere from Kenya to South Africa, the Okavango flood is in, the migration is in the Mara and the gorilla trails are at their driest. It is also the most expensive time and needs booking far ahead. June is the best-value alternative.

faqs.q: Is the green season worth it?
faqs.a: Yes, for the right traveler. Rates can be far below peak, the landscape is lush, there are young animals and excellent birds, and you may have sightings to yourself. Expect some rain, thicker bush and less predictable game, and choose a private reserve with good guides.

faqs.q: When should I avoid going on safari?
faqs.a: April and May in Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda and Uganda, when the long rains fall, and January to March in Zambia and Zimbabwe, when many camps are closed. Even then, parts of South Africa and Namibia remain good choices.

page.question: What is daily life like on a world cruise, and who actually enjoys one?
page.title: Daily Life on a World Cruise: An Honest Picture, and Who Actually Enjoys It
page.description: What four months at sea are really like: sea days and port days, the community on board, medical care and its limits, internet, food fatigue, overland trips and coming home. Who thrives on a world cruise, and who is restless by week six.
page.capsule: A world cruise is less a long holiday than a few months of living somewhere unusual. Days at sea outnumber what most people expect, and they settle into a routine of lectures, exercise, classes, meals and friends. People who enjoy routine, company and the sea thrive. Independent travelers who want long stays ashore are often restless by the sixth week.
answer: A full world cruise lasts roughly four to six months, and on many routes close to half the days are spent at sea. That is the fact that decides whether you will like it. The port days are the reason people book: sixty or more places, from Sydney to Cape Town, without a single flight. The sea days are the reason people come back. By the third week the ship has stopped being a hotel and become a neighborhood. You have a table, a walking circuit on deck, a favorite seat in the observation lounge, a bridge partner and opinions about the lecturers. The crew know how you take your coffee. For many guests this settled, sociable rhythm is the pleasure of the thing, and the ports are punctuation.

It is also why some people should not go. Most port calls last eight to ten hours, with an overnight stay in a few major cities. You will see a great deal of the world and none of it deeply. If your idea of travel is a week in one place, a rented car and no plan, a world cruise will frustrate you. Our atlas holds {{collection:worldcruise}} {{page:/journeys/worldcruise|world cruises and segments}}, {{journeys:collection=worldcruise&daysMin=100}} of them voyages of a hundred days or more, and a segment of three or four weeks is the sensible way to find out which kind of traveler you are.

paras: The sixth week is when it tells. The novelty has worn off, home feels far away, and there are still three months to go. Guests who have built a life on board barely notice. Guests who were waiting for the trip to entertain them start counting days. Almost every world cruiser can name someone who left the ship in Singapore or Cape Town, and most say they could have predicted it.

sections.h2: The practical realities
list: The community: lines treat full-voyage guests as a group apart, with their own events ashore, gala evenings and often laundry, Wi-Fi and a shipboard credit included. Friendships form quickly and many guests rebook together.

Solo travelers: a world cruise is one of the easiest long trips to take alone. Hosted tables, classes and, on some lines, dance hosts and bridge instructors mean you are alone only when you choose to be.

Medical care: every ship has a doctor, nurses and a small medical centre. They handle everyday illness and can stabilize an emergency, but they are not a hospital. Serious problems mean leaving the ship at the next port, or an evacuation, which is very costly without insurance. Bring every prescription for the whole voyage plus spare.

Internet: satellite service is now good enough on most ships for email, banking and video calls with the family, with slow patches in remote ocean. You can stay in touch; you may not want to work a full day.
Fitness and weight: the food is constant and excellent. Guests who do well treat the gym, the deck and the stairs as part of the day from the first week.

Food fatigue: even very good menus repeat over four months. Ships counter it with guest chefs, regional menus, local produce taken on in port and several restaurants. Eating ashore whenever you can is the better cure.

Overland excursions: the big inland sights, the Taj Mahal, Angkor, Machu Picchu, a safari, are reached by leaving the ship for two to five nights and rejoining it at a later port. They are expensive and worth it, and they break the routine at the right moment.
Your suite: over four months, space, storage and a balcony matter far more than on a week's cruise. This is the trip on which to stretch for the better category.

sections.h2: Coming home
paras: Nobody warns you about the return. After months in which every meal appeared, every bed was made and every day had a shape, an empty house and a full inbox are a shock. Guests commonly describe a few flat weeks, and missing people they saw daily for a third of a year. It passes, and it is a sign the voyage worked. Many have the next one booked before they disembark, which is why world cruises sell out so far ahead. Give yourself a quiet fortnight afterward, and plan something to look forward to.

faqs.q: Do people get bored on a world cruise?
faqs.a: Some do, usually those who expected the ship to keep them busy. Guests who bring interests of their own, or take up the classes, lectures and games on offer, rarely are. Trying a segment of three or four weeks first is the reliable way to find out before committing to four months.

faqs.q: Is a world cruise good for solo travelers?
faqs.a: Yes. It is one of the most sociable ways to travel alone, with a stable community, hosted dining and daily activities. Single supplements are significant, though some lines offer reduced supplements or a small number of solo suites, and those sell first.

faqs.q: What happens if you get sick on a world cruise?
faqs.a: The ship's medical centre treats everyday illness and injuries on board, at a charge. Anything serious means disembarking for hospital care at the next suitable port, or a medical evacuation. Comprehensive travel insurance with evacuation cover is not optional on a voyage of this length.

page.question: La Dolce Vita Orient Express or the Venice Simplon-Orient-Express?
page.title: La Dolce Vita Orient Express vs the Venice Simplon-Orient-Express: Two Trains, One Name
page.description: Two different trains run by two different companies. The Venice Simplon-Orient-Express is Belmond's restored 1920s train across Europe; La Dolce Vita Orient Express is a new Italian train from Rome. Routes, cabins, bathrooms, atmosphere and who each suits.
page.capsule: They are different trains from different companies. The Venice Simplon-Orient-Express, run by Belmond, is the restored 1920s train between Paris and Venice, with black tie and vintage carriages. La Dolce Vita Orient Express is a new train with 1960s Italian design, running round trips from Rome. Choose the first for history and ceremony, the second for comfort, private bathrooms and Italy.
answer: The shared name causes real confusion, so start there. The Venice Simplon-Orient-Express belongs to {{op:train/Belmond Trains|Belmond}} and has run since the 1980s using original sleeping and dining cars from the 1920s and 1930s. La Dolce Vita Orient Express is a separate venture, launched in 2025 under the Orient Express brand that the hotel group Accor is reviving, with the Italian company Arsenale. One company does not operate the other's train, tickets are not interchangeable, and the experiences have little in common beyond a good dinner on rails.

The Belmond train is a period piece. You travel in marquetry-panelled compartments, dress for dinner and cross borders overnight, most famously between Paris and Venice. {{op:train/La Dolce Vita Orient Express|La Dolce Vita}} is a modern luxury train dressed in the style of 1960s Italy, with cabins built for comfort, and it stays within Italy on journeys of one or two nights that begin in Rome. Our atlas holds {{journeys:vessel=Venice Simplon-Orient-Express}} itineraries on the Venice Simplon-Orient-Express and {{journeys:operator=La Dolce Vita Orient Express}} on La Dolce Vita.

paras: The bathroom is the practical difference that decides it for many people. On the Venice Simplon-Orient-Express the original Historic Cabins have no private toilet or shower, and you pay a large premium for a Suite or Grand Suite to get one. On La Dolce Vita every cabin has its own bathroom. If the idea of a shared lavatory at the end of the corridor spoils the romance for you, that settles it, unless you book the Belmond train's suites.

The other difference is the journey itself. The Belmond train goes somewhere: you fall asleep in France and wake in the Alps, and arriving in Venice by rail is the point. La Dolce Vita mostly returns to Rome, so it is an excursion from the city, a way to see Tuscany, Venice or the south in style without packing and unpacking. Treat it as two nights of a longer Italian trip.

sections.h2: Which to choose
list: For a big anniversary or a lifelong wish to ride the Orient Express: the Venice Simplon-Orient-Express. It is the one people mean, and the ritual is the pleasure.
If you sleep lightly or want a proper bathroom without paying for a suite: La Dolce Vita.
If you are already planning Italy: La Dolce Vita fits between Rome and a week elsewhere. Stay in Rome the night before, since departures are from the city.
If you want to link Paris or London with Italy: the Venice Simplon-Orient-Express, with hotel nights at each end.
For food and wine above all: both are strong. La Dolce Vita's routes lean on regional Italian cooking and vineyards; the Belmond train's dining cars are part of its legend.
For the lowest fare that still feels special: a Historic Cabin on the Belmond train's one-night routes is usually the entry point, with the trade-offs above.
paras: Both sell their best cabins many months ahead, and both run mainly from spring to autumn, with a few winter and festive departures. Neither is a way to get from one place to another. Each is an evening, a night and a morning that you would remember, and the question is only which kind of evening you would enjoy more. The {{page:/answers/venice-simplon-orient-express-worth-it|Venice Simplon-Orient-Express answer}} goes through that train's cabins and the night on board in detail.

faqs.q: Is La Dolce Vita Orient Express the real Orient Express?
faqs.a: It is a new train carrying the historic Orient Express name, which now belongs to the hotel group Accor. It is not the Venice Simplon-Orient-Express, which is Belmond's train of restored original carriages. Both are legitimate; they are simply different companies, trains and routes.

faqs.q: Which train has private bathrooms?
faqs.a: La Dolce Vita Orient Express has a private bathroom with shower in every cabin and suite. On the Venice Simplon-Orient-Express only the Suites and Grand Suites have private bathrooms; the Historic Cabins have a washbasin and shared toilets, with no shower.

faqs.q: Can you combine the two trains in one trip?
faqs.a: Yes, with planning. Take the Venice Simplon-Orient-Express from Paris to Venice, spend some days in Venice and Florence, travel to Rome and join La Dolce Vita for a one- or two-night journey. Dates need lining up well ahead, since neither train runs daily.

page.description: A small-ship cruise against island-hopping by ferry: what each gives you, the Cyclades against the Dodecanese and the Ionian, how many islands fit in a week, the meltemi and the season, across the {{journeys:collection=yacht&region=AEGEAN}} Aegean yacht itineraries in our atlas.
page.capsule: Take a yacht cruise to see five or six Greek islands in a week without packing, ferries or transfers, including small islands that are awkward to reach. Take ferries and hotels to stay longer on two or three islands, with evenings ashore and your own pace. The best trip often combines them: a few hotel nights in Athens or on Santorini, then a week at sea.
answer: Both ways work, and they produce different holidays. A yacht-style cruise is a moving hotel. You unpack once, wake at a new island most mornings, swim off the back of the ship and never look at a ferry timetable. In a week you might see Mykonos, Santorini, Paros, Patmos, Hydra and a quiet anchorage you had never heard of. What you give up is time: a day in port, sometimes an evening, then the ship moves on. Our atlas holds {{journeys:collection=yacht&region=AEGEAN}} {{page:/journeys/yacht|yacht itineraries in the Aegean}}, most of seven to ten nights.

Island-hopping by ferry is slower and deeper. Three or four nights on an island is long enough to find a beach you like, a taverna that knows you and a morning with nothing planned. The price is logistics. Every move costs most of a day once you count checking out, the port, the crossing and checking in, and in July and August the meltemi, the strong northerly wind of the Aegean summer, can delay or cancel fast ferries. The more islands you try to fit in, the more of the holiday you spend in transit. That is why the usual advice is two islands in a week, three at the very most.

paras: The famous islands are where a ship's limits show most. At Santorini every ship anchors in the caldera and guests go ashore by tender to the old port below Fira, then queue for the cable car on busy days, and Greece now charges cruise passengers a levy that is highest there and at Mykonos in summer. A small ship softens this, with fewer people to land and often a later stay, but if Santorini is the reason for your trip, sleep there. A hotel on the caldera rim after the day visitors leave is a different island.

The small islands are where a ship wins. Places such as Folegandros, Symi, Amorgos or Ithaca are a long way round by ferry and trivial for a yacht. A cruise is the easiest way to see the Greece that most visitors never reach.

July and August bring heat, crowds, peak prices and the meltemi, so if school dates fix you there, favor the Ionian islands or Crete for a land stay, and expect a cruise captain to adjust the route.

Combining the two is the answer for many people. Spend two nights in Athens, at {{hotel:Hotel Grande Bretagne, a Luxury Collection Hotel, Athens|the Grande Bretagne}} or on the coast, see the Acropolis, then sail for a week. Or finish the voyage and stay three nights on Santorini, Mykonos or Paros, where the villa atlas also holds {{villas:destination=Greece}} {{page:/atlas/villa|homes}}. You get the range of a cruise and at least one island properly.

faqs.q: How many Greek islands can you visit in a week by ferry?
faqs.a: Two comfortably, three if they are close together, such as Paros, Naxos and Santorini. Each move takes most of a day. Travelers who try four or five in a week by ferry spend much of the holiday in ports, which is the case for a cruise.

faqs.q: Is a Greek islands cruise rough?
faqs.a: Usually not, but the Aegean can be lively in July and August when the meltemi blows, and small ships feel it more than large ones. June and September are calmer. If you are prone to seasickness, choose those months, a midship cabin, or an Ionian itinerary.

faqs.q: Should I fly or take the ferry between islands?
faqs.a: Fly between Athens and the islands when time is short; flights take under an hour. Take ferries between neighboring islands, where they are quick and frequent. There are few direct flights from one island to another, so most routes go back through Athens.

page.question: Croatia and the Adriatic by yacht: what do you see that big ships miss?
page.title: Croatia and the Adriatic by Yacht: The Ports Big Ships Miss
page.description: Why the Dalmatian coast suits small ships: Hvar, Korčula, Vis, Šibenik and Rovinj against the large-ship ports of Dubrovnik and Split, with port limits, typical routes and the season, across the {{journeys:collection=yacht&region=ADRIATIC}} Adriatic yacht itineraries in our atlas.
page.capsule: A yacht-sized ship on the Adriatic reaches the island towns that large ships skip: Hvar, Korčula, Vis, Šibenik and Rovinj. It also handles the big ports better, arriving at Dubrovnik and Kotor early or staying late, when the crowds have gone. Sail in late May, June or September, and add hotel nights in Dubrovnik or Venice at either end.
answer: The Croatian coast is more than a thousand islands and a string of small stone towns built by Venice, and very little of it was made for large ships. The big vessels call at Dubrovnik, Split, Kotor in Montenegro and sometimes Zadar, because those are the ports that can take them. The places that make the coast special are in between: Hvar's harbor under its fortress, the walled peninsula of Korčula, Vis far out to sea, Šibenik at the end of a narrow channel, Rovinj on the Istrian coast. A yacht-style ship anchors off them or ties up in town, and its guests step ashore into the old town.

Size also changes the famous ports. Dubrovnik's old town is small, and when several large ships are in, the main street is shoulder to shoulder by mid-morning, which is why the city now limits how many may call at once. A small ship can time it differently: arrive for the early morning, or stay into the evening, when the walls and the limestone streets are close to empty. paras: Venice is the other place where size now matters. Large cruise ships have been barred from the Giudecca Canal and St. Mark's Basin since 2021 and use mainland terminals or other ports altogether, with a transfer into the city. Smaller ships may still berth close to the historic center. If sailing into or out of Venice is part of the appeal, check exactly where your ship docks.

Along the Croatian coast the tender rides are short and the water is sheltered by the islands, so this is one of the calmest and easiest regions for a small ship. It is also one of the best for swimming from the marina, since the sea is clear and warm from June.

sections.h2: Routes, season and hotels at either end
paras: Most yacht itineraries here are one-way or loops of seven to ten nights. The classic line runs between Venice and Dubrovnik, sometimes continuing south past Montenegro and Corfu to Athens. Others are round trips from Dubrovnik or Venice that stay within Croatia and Montenegro. One-way routes cover more ground. Round trips make flights simpler.

The season is May to October. Late May, June and September are the best of it: warm sea, long evenings, room in the harbors. July and August are hot and very busy, in Dubrovnik and Hvar above all, and that is when a small ship's ability to arrive early and leave late is worth the most. April and late October are quiet and cooler, with some island restaurants closed.

Give yourself nights ashore at each end. In Dubrovnik, {{hotel:Villa Dubrovnik}} sits on the rocks just outside the walls. On Hvar, {{hotel:Maslina Resort}} and {{hotel:Palace Elisabeth, Hvar Heritage Hotel|Palace Elisabeth}} let you see the island after the day boats leave. In Istria, {{hotel:Grand Park Hotel Rovinj}} faces the old town across the harbor. In Venice, {{hotel:Aman Venice}} and {{hotel:The Gritti Palace, a Luxury Collection Hotel, Venice|The Gritti Palace}} are on the Grand Canal. The atlas lists {{hotels:country=Croatia}} {{page:/hotels/croatia|hotels in Croatia}}.
list: First visit: a Venice to Dubrovnik route covers Istria, the islands and both great cities.
Swimmers and families: choose an itinerary with several island anchorages, such as Hvar, Vis and Mljet, over one with a city every day.
Repeat visitors: look for Vis, Šibenik, Lastovo or the Kornati, which the classic routes skip.
History: Split, Dubrovnik and Kotor are essential, and a small ship lets you see them at the right hours.

faqs.q: Is Croatia better by yacht cruise or by land?
faqs.a: By sea, if you want the islands. The coast road is slow and the ferries take planning, while a ship links Hvar, Korčula, Vis and Dubrovnik overnight. A land trip suits those who want several days in one place, or inland sights such as Plitvice and Istria's hill towns.

faqs.q: Do cruise ships still go to Dubrovnik and Venice?
faqs.a: Yes, with restrictions. Dubrovnik limits how many large ships and passengers can call at once. Venice bars large ships from the historic center, so they dock on the mainland or at other ports. Small ships are less affected and often berth closer to town.

faqs.q: When is the best month for an Adriatic cruise?
faqs.a: June or September. The sea is warm enough to swim, the days are long and the ports are far less crowded than in July and August. Late May is a good choice for sightseeing, with cooler water.

page.question: Is the Royal Scotsman worth it, and which route should you take?
page.title: Is the Royal Scotsman Worth It? What the Train Is Like and Which Route to Take
page.description: Belmond's Royal Scotsman explained: a small train from Edinburgh with en-suite cabins, a spa car and an open observation deck, the routes by length, what is included, and how it compares with driving the Highlands, across {{journeys:vessel=Royal Scotsman}} itineraries in our atlas.
page.capsule: Yes, for travelers who want the Highlands with everything arranged and good company at dinner. The Royal Scotsman carries about forty guests from Edinburgh in en-suite cabins, stops at night so you sleep still, and includes meals, drinks and excursions. Take four nights for the best balance. It is a poor fit for anyone who wants independence or long walks.
answer: The Royal Scotsman is a house party on rails. {{op:train/Belmond Trains|Belmond}} runs it from Edinburgh between roughly April and October, with about forty guests, a crew that outnumbers most small hotels' and a route through the parts of Scotland that are hardest to see well by yourself. The cabins are wood-panelled and compact, all with their own shower and toilet. There are two dining cars, a spa carriage, and an observation car with an open veranda at the back, where most guests end up with a whisky as the lochs go by. At night the train is stabled at a quiet station or siding, so unlike most sleeper trains you sleep without motion.

What you are paying for is the organization and the access. Days include visits to distilleries, castles and private estates, often hosted by the people who own them, with a coach waiting at the platform and nothing to arrange. Evenings are long dinners at shared or private tables, followed by music in the observation car. Our atlas holds {{journeys:vessel=Royal Scotsman}} {{page:/journeys/train|Royal Scotsman itineraries}}. Fares are very high for the nights involved, and they include nearly everything: all meals, wines and spirits, and the excursions.

page.question: How do you get to Machu Picchu in luxury: Hiram Bingham, Andean Explorer, or neither?
page.title: Machu Picchu in Luxury: Hiram Bingham, Andean Explorer, or Neither?
page.description: The two Belmond trains in Peru untangled: the Hiram Bingham day train to Machu Picchu and the Andean Explorer sleeper to Lake Titicaca and Arequipa, with the alternatives, altitude, site entry and a sensible order for a week.
page.capsule: The Hiram Bingham is the luxury train to Machu Picchu: a day service with meals, a bar car and an observation deck. The Andean Explorer is a sleeper across the high plateau to Lake Titicaca and Arequipa, and does not go to Machu Picchu. Take the Hiram Bingham one way, a panoramic train the other, and start in the Sacred Valley for the altitude.
answer: People confuse the two because both are {{op:train/Belmond Peruvian Trains|Belmond}} trains that leave from the Cusco area. They do different jobs. The Hiram Bingham is a day train between the Cusco area and Aguas Calientes, the small town below Machu Picchu, taking about three and a half hours each way along the Urubamba River. It has 1920s-style dining cars, a bar car with live music and an open observation car, and a meal is served in each direction. The Andean Explorer is a sleeper train with cabins, a spa car and a piano bar, running one- or two-night journeys from Cusco across the altiplano to Lake Titicaca and on to Arequipa. It is a trip in its own right, added before or after Machu Picchu. Our atlas holds {{journeys:operator=Belmond Peruvian Trains}} itineraries on the two.

No road reaches Machu Picchu. Everyone arrives at Aguas Calientes by train, or on foot along the Inca Trail, and then takes a bus up the switchbacks to the entrance. So the real question is which train. The Hiram Bingham is the most comfortable and by far the most expensive. The panoramic day trains run by PeruRail and Inca Rail cover the same track, through the same gorge, for a fraction of the fare. A good plan uses both: a panoramic train down from the Sacred Valley, a night near the site, and the Hiram Bingham back to Cusco, when dinner and a pisco sour are welcome.

paras: Entry to the site is controlled. Tickets are sold for a set time and a fixed one-way circuit, daily numbers are capped, and a licensed guide is required. The circuits differ in what they include, and the classic postcard view is on some and not others, so the choice matters. The rules have changed several times in recent years. Buy tickets well ahead, in high season months ahead, and let whoever arranges the trip match the circuit to the train.

Stay a night if you can. Day trippers arrive late in the morning with everyone else. Guests who sleep in Aguas Calientes, at {{hotel:Inkaterra Machu Picchu Pueblo Hotel}} or {{hotel:SUMAQ Machu Picchu Hotel|Sumaq}}, or at {{hotel:Sanctuary Lodge, A Belmond Hotel, Machu Picchu|Sanctuary Lodge}}, the only hotel at the entrance, can go up for the first entry of the day and again in the late afternoon, when the site is quiet.

sections.h2: Altitude, season and a sensible week
paras: Altitude shapes the order of the trip. Cusco is at about 11,000 feet, and flying in from sea level and staying there is how people lose their first two days to headaches. The Sacred Valley is roughly 2,000 feet lower and Machu Picchu lower still, at about 8,000 feet. So go down first: drive from Cusco airport straight to the valley, spend two or three nights there, visit Machu Picchu, and finish in Cusco once you have adjusted.

The dry season runs from May to September, with clear days, cold nights and the most visitors in June, July and August. April, May, September and October are the best compromise. From November to March it rains, heavily from January, the Inca Trail closes each February and trains are sometimes disrupted, though the site stays open and is greener and emptier.
list: Days 1 to 3: the Sacred Valley, at {{hotel:Rio Sagrado, A Belmond Hotel, Sacred Valley|Rio Sagrado}}, {{hotel:Explora Valle Sagrado}}, {{hotel:Sol y Luna}} or {{hotel:Tambo del Inka, a Luxury Collection Resort & Spa, Valle Sagrado|Tambo del Inka}}, which has its own station. See Pisac, Ollantaytambo, Moray and the salt pans.
Day 4: a panoramic train to Aguas Calientes and an afternoon entry to Machu Picchu. Night near the site.
Day 5: early entry on a second circuit, then the Hiram Bingham to Cusco with dinner on board.
Days 6 and 7: Cusco, at {{hotel:Palacio Nazarenas, A Belmond Hotel, Cusco|Palacio Nazarenas}} or {{hotel:Monasterio, A Belmond Hotel, Cusco|Monasterio}}. The cathedral, San Blas, Sacsayhuamán.
With three more days: the Andean Explorer from Cusco to Lake Titicaca and Arequipa, then fly to Lima.

sections.h2: Is the Andean Explorer worth adding?
paras: Yes, if you have the time and have already adjusted to the altitude. It is one of the highest railways in the world, crossing a pass at around 14,000 feet, and the landscape is enormous: empty plateau, herds of alpaca, snow peaks, then the lake. Cabins have private bathrooms, there is an open observation car at the back, and the stops include Lake Titicaca's islands and, on the longer route, the country around the Colca Canyon. Do it after Cusco, never straight from the coast, because you sleep at altitude. It suits travelers who have a fortnight in Peru. With only a week, spend the time in the valley and at Machu Picchu instead.

faqs.q: Does the Andean Explorer go to Machu Picchu?
faqs.a: No. The Andean Explorer is a sleeper train between Cusco, Lake Titicaca and Arequipa. The Belmond train to Machu Picchu is the Hiram Bingham, a day service. They are often confused because both are Belmond trains departing from the Cusco area.

faqs.q: Is the Hiram Bingham worth the money?
faqs.a: For a celebration, or as the journey back after a long day at the site, yes. The food, the music and the observation car turn a transfer into an evening. As transport it is poor value, since panoramic trains follow the same line for far less. Taking it one way is the sensible middle.

faqs.q: How do you avoid altitude sickness on a Machu Picchu trip?
faqs.a: Start low and climb. Go from Cusco airport directly to the Sacred Valley, rest on the first day, drink water, avoid alcohol and heavy meals at first, and leave Cusco for the end. Ask your doctor about medication before you travel if you have had trouble at altitude before.
