page.question: Booking a villa through a travel advisor vs. Airbnb or Vrbo: what is actually different?
page.title: Villa Through a Travel Advisor vs. Airbnb or Vrbo: What Is Actually Different
page.description: An honest comparison of a vetted villa program with a rental platform: inspection, local managers, staff and what happens when something goes wrong, against choice, price and flexibility. When a platform is the sensible choice, and when it is not.
page.capsule: A platform gives you the widest choice, lower price points and instant booking, and leaves the checking to you. A villa booked through an advisor comes from a managed program: the home has been inspected, a local manager meets you, staff and provisioning are arranged, and someone answers when the air conditioning fails. For a short, simple stay, use a platform. For a large group or costly week, do not.
answer: The two are selling different things. Airbnb and Vrbo are marketplaces. They list millions of homes, show reviews, take payment and step back, and the stay is between you and the owner or host. A villa program is closer to a hotel company without a building. It selects a few thousand homes, sends its own people to inspect them, signs a contract with each owner, and employs or appoints a manager on the ground. Our villa atlas draws on programs of that kind and holds {{collection:villa}} {{page:/atlas/villa|homes}}. You have less to choose from, and what you choose has been seen by someone whose job depends on it being as described.

For most trips the difference only shows when something goes wrong. The pool is green, the hot water fails on the second day, the owner sells the house two months before you arrive, a storm closes the airport. On a platform you message the host and, if that fails, open a case and wait. With a managed villa there is a local person with a phone, a list of tradesmen and other houses in the portfolio. Paying ten or twenty thousand dollars for a week with eleven relatives is the situation in which that matters. For a two-night stay in a city apartment it does not.

paras: The useful question is what happens on the worst day of the trip, and who you will call. If you would be content to sort it out yourself, a platform is fine and often cheaper. If the answer needs to be someone else, book a home that comes with that someone.

faqs.q: Is it more expensive to book a villa through a travel advisor?
faqs.a: Usually not. The advisor is paid a commission by the villa company, so the rate is typically the same as booking that company direct. What can be higher is the kind of home: managed programs carry few inexpensive properties compared with a platform.

faqs.q: Are the villas on Airbnb and in villa programs the same homes?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Some owners list on both. The difference is what comes with the booking: inspection, a local manager, arranged staff and help if things go wrong come from the villa company, not from the house.

faqs.q: What happens if a villa is cancelled by the owner?
faqs.a: On a platform you receive a refund and look again, often at short notice and higher prices. A villa company will normally try to move you to a comparable home in its portfolio. Neither can guarantee an equal replacement in a peak week, which is one more reason to insure the trip.

page.question: TCS World Travel, Abercrombie & Kent or National Geographic: which private jet journey?

page.description: The operators behind private jet journeys compared: aircraft and group size, style, length and who each suits, including Safrans du Monde, Remote Lands and Blue Parallel, across the {{collection:jet}} jet itineraries in our atlas.

Choose Abercrombie & Kent for a small group with strong guiding on the ground. Choose National Geographic for learning, with experts and photographers aboard and a larger group. For one region in depth with very few fellow travelers, look at Remote Lands in Asia or Blue Parallel in Latin America.
answer: A private jet journey is a group tour in which the aircraft is chartered for the whole trip: one plane, one crew, direct flights between places that would otherwise take two or three connections, and luggage that moves without you. {{page:/answers/private-jet-journeys-explained|How these trips work}} is covered separately. Once you have decided you want one, the question is whose, because the operators differ more than their brochures suggest. Three run the large around-the-world programs on converted airliners: TCS World Travel, Abercrombie & Kent and National Geographic. Three more work at a smaller scale: Safrans du Monde from France, Remote Lands in Asia and Blue Parallel in Latin America.

sections.h2: How to choose
list: Decide what the trip is for. Seeing the great sights in comfort points to TCS. Understanding them points to National Geographic. Meeting them through local people points to Abercrombie & Kent.

Around the world, or one region? World tours cover eight to ten stops in three to four weeks with long flights between. Regional journeys, Africa, the Silk Road, Asia, South America, go deeper with shorter flights.
Look at the pace. Two nights at each stop is common and tiring over three weeks. Itineraries with some three-night stays are kinder.
Check the hotels by name. The best departures use the leading hotel at each stop; in remote places there may be only one acceptable choice.
Ask about the seat. Flat beds matter on the long sectors of a world tour and less on short regional hops.
Ask who travels with you. The large programs carry an expedition leader, staff and a physician. Smaller ones may not.
Traveling alone? Single supplements are substantial. Some operators offer a few reduced-supplement places that go early.
paras: These trips sell twelve to eighteen months ahead and the most popular, the classic around-the-world routes, often carry a waitlist. They are also among the few journeys where an advisor's knowledge of the individual departures is worth more than any published comparison, since the same operator's itineraries differ a good deal from one another.

faqs.q: Which private jet journey is the most luxurious?
faqs.a: TCS World Travel's programs, including the Four Seasons Private Jet, are generally considered the most comfortable in the air and the most hotel-focused on the ground. For privacy, the small-jet journeys from Remote Lands and Blue Parallel carry far fewer guests.

faqs.q: How many people travel on a private jet tour?
faqs.a: It depends on the operator: about 75 on National Geographic's jet, about 48 to 50 on TCS World Travel's and Abercrombie & Kent's, and fewer than twenty on the smaller aircraft used by regional specialists. Ask for the figure on the specific departure.

faqs.q: Are private jet journeys worth the cost?
faqs.a: For travelers short of time who want remote places linked without connections, yes: a three-week itinerary would take twice as long on scheduled flights. If you are happy to travel slowly, the same hotels and guides can be arranged privately for less.

page.question: Is a Ritz-Carlton yacht cruise worth it, and should you choose Evrima, Ilma or Luminara?
page.title: Is a Ritz-Carlton Yacht Cruise Worth It? Evrima vs Ilma vs Luminara
page.description: An honest verdict on the Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection: who it suits, what the fare includes, how the three yachts differ and where each sails, across {{journeys:operator=Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection}} itineraries in our atlas.
page.capsule: Yes, for travelers who like resort hotels and are wary of cruises: every suite has a terrace, the fare includes dining and drinks, and itineraries favor small harbors and late evenings. Choose Evrima for the most intimate ship, Ilma or Luminara for more space and restaurants, then pick by where each sails. Cruise traditionalists who want lectures, shows and long voyages get more elsewhere.
answer: The Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection was the first of the hotel brands to go to sea, and several seasons on it is the most proven of them. The idea is a Ritz-Carlton resort that moves. There are no inside cabins, no formal nights, no assigned tables and no casino. Days are built around the port, the pool and the marina at the stern, which opens for swimming and paddleboarding when the yacht is at anchor. Evenings are a choice of restaurants and a bar with live music. People who have never wanted to take a cruise tend to like it very much. People who love traditional cruising sometimes find it quiet.

It costs more per night than the classic luxury lines, and the fair question is what the premium buys. The answer is the space per guest, a terrace on every suite, itineraries with more small ports and overnight stays, and an atmosphere with no cruise-ship habits at all. If those matter to you, it is worth it. If you mainly want to see many places in comfort, a Seabourn or Silversea suite does that for less. Our atlas holds {{journeys:operator=Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection}} {{op:yacht/Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection|Ritz-Carlton}} itineraries with {{departures:operator=Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection}} departures.

faqs.q: Is a Ritz-Carlton yacht good for families?

page.question: Glacier Express or Bernina Express: which Swiss scenic train, and which class?
page.title: Glacier Express vs Bernina Express: Which Swiss Scenic Train, and Which Class
page.description: Switzerland's two famous panoramic trains compared: route, length, scenery and classes, including Excellence Class, with seat reservations, which side to sit on, winter against summer and how to join them into a week.
page.capsule: Take the Bernina Express if you have time for only one: it is shorter, about four hours, and crosses the highest and most dramatic line in the Alps. Take the Glacier Express for a full day of travel in comfort between Zermatt and St. Moritz, in Excellence Class if you want the meal and a guaranteed window. With a week, do both; they meet in the Engadin.
answer: They are different kinds of journey that happen to share a region and a railway company. The Glacier Express is a whole day, about eight hours, between Zermatt and St. Moritz. It crosses the Oberalp Pass, runs through the Rhine Gorge and over the Landwasser Viaduct, and is as much about being looked after on a train as about any one view. It calls itself the slowest express in the world. The Bernina Express is half the length, about four hours from Chur or two and a half from St. Moritz, and it climbs over the Bernina Pass in the open air, past glaciers and lakes, then spirals down two thousand meters into Italy at Tirano. Mile for mile it is the more spectacular of the two.

So the choice turns on time and temperament. If you enjoy a long lunch as the country goes by, the Glacier Express is a pleasure, and Excellence Class makes it a real occasion. If you get restless after four hours, or the weather is doubtful, the Bernina gives you more drama in less time, and you can do it there and back in a day from St. Moritz. Both are ordinary scheduled trains with panoramic cars, not private luxury trains, so they fit into a trip built around hotels. The fare supplement includes a multi-course meal with wine, a bar in the carriage and a host for the day. It is expensive and it sells out, particularly in summer. First class has the same windows with seats two and one across, and you order lunch at your seat. Second class has the same view with four seats across.

The Bernina Express has first and second class in panoramic cars, with a trolley for drinks and snacks and no dining car. First class is worth it mainly for space. Regional trains run the same line every hour with ordinary carriages and windows that open, which photographers prefer, and they need no reservation.

sections.h2: Reservations, seats and seasons
list: Reservations: both trains require a seat reservation, paid on top of the ticket. A Swiss Travel Pass covers the fare on both and does not cover the reservation or the Excellence Class supplement.
Book ahead: summer and the Christmas weeks fill. Excellence Class can sell out months in advance.
Which side: on the Bernina Express heading south, the right-hand side has the better of the glacier and the spiral viaduct. On the Glacier Express the view changes sides all day, and both are good.
Whole route or part: the finest stretch of the Glacier Express is between Andermatt and St. Moritz. Travelers short of time can ride half and still see the best of it.
Winter: both run through deep snow and are beautiful on a clear day, with short daylight. The Glacier Express pauses for some weeks in late autumn.
Summer: long days, green valleys, open hiking trails at each end. The busiest season.
Weather: panoramic windows show cloud as well as mountains. Keep the date flexible if you can, and remember there is no opening window in the panoramic cars.

sections.h2: Joining them into a week
paras: The two trains meet in the Engadin, which makes a simple and very good week. Start in Zermatt, with two or three nights under the Matterhorn at {{hotel:Mont Cervin Palace Zermatt|Mont Cervin Palace}} or {{hotel:Grand Hotel Zermatterhof}}. Take the Glacier Express east, breaking the journey at {{hotel:The Chedi Andermatt}} if eight hours in one sitting is too much. Spend two or three nights in St. Moritz, at {{hotel:Badrutt's Palace Hotel}} or {{hotel:Kulm Hotel St. Moritz}}. Then ride the Bernina Express over the pass to Tirano.

From Tirano you are in Italy, and a regional train reaches Lake Como in about an hour and a half, which is a fine way to finish. To stay in Switzerland instead, return over the pass and continue to Lucerne or Zurich. Luggage can be sent ahead between Swiss stations, so you travel with a day bag. faqs.a: For a celebration or a once-only trip, yes. Every seat is a window seat, and the meal, wine and service fill the day well. If you mainly want the scenery, first class shows you exactly the same view for much less.

faqs.q: Can you do the Glacier Express and Bernina Express in one trip?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is the best way to see both. Ride the Glacier Express from Zermatt to St. Moritz, stay two nights, then take the Bernina Express to Tirano. Doing both on consecutive days without a pause in St. Moritz is too much sitting.

faqs.a: No, you can buy point-to-point tickets. A pass covers the fare on both trains and is good value if you are also using trains, boats and buses elsewhere. Either way you must pay for a seat reservation separately.

page.question: French Polynesia: Bora Bora resort, a Tahiti cruise, or both?
page.title: French Polynesia: Bora Bora Resort, a Tahiti Cruise, or Both?
page.description: A resort stay against a small-ship cruise through the Society Islands, and the case for combining them: the islands compared, what a ship reaches, overwater bungalow reality, flights and seasons, with the {{hotels:country=French Polynesia}} resorts in our atlas.
page.capsule: Do both if you have ten nights or more: a week on a small ship to see Moorea, Taha'a, Bora Bora and the atolls, then three or four nights in an overwater bungalow to stop. With a week only, choose the cruise for variety and value, or a resort for rest and privacy. Bora Bora alone shows you one lagoon of many.
answer: French Polynesia is 118 islands spread over an area the size of Western Europe, and most visitors see two of them. The classic trip is a flight to Tahiti, a short hop to Bora Bora and a week in an overwater bungalow. It is a lovely week. It is also expensive, quiet, and limited to one lagoon. A resort stay is the right choice for a honeymoon or for anyone whose main aim is to do very little in a beautiful place: {{hotel:Four Seasons Resort Bora Bora}}, {{hotel:The St. Regis Bora Bora Resort}} and {{hotel:Conrad Bora Bora Nui}} on Bora Bora, {{hotel:Le Taha'a}} on its own islet, or {{hotel:The Brando}} on the private atoll of Tetiaroa.

A small ship shows you what the islands are actually like, and how different they are from each other. In seven nights from Papeete you can see Moorea's sharp green peaks, the vanilla farms of Taha'a, Bora Bora's lagoon and Huahine, with no inter-island flights and no packing. Longer voyages add the Tuamotus, flat coral atolls with some of the best diving in the Pacific, and the remote Marquesas. {{op:cruise/Paul Gauguin Cruises|Paul Gauguin}} is the specialist, with {{journeys:operator=Paul Gauguin Cruises}} itineraries in our atlas on a ship built for these lagoons. Lindblad and PONANT run expedition voyages here, the Ritz-Carlton yacht Evrima has a season, and Silversea and Seabourn pass through on longer Pacific sailings.

paras: If you combine them, sail first. The cruise is the busy part, and it tells you which island you would like to return to. Finishing in a bungalow means the last days of the trip are the restful ones before the long flight home.

An honest word on overwater bungalows. They are worth doing once. The pleasure is stepping from your deck into warm, clear water and watching the light change on the lagoon. What surprises people is the price of everything once there, since every meal is at the resort, and that the best view, toward Mount Otemanu on Bora Bora, belongs to some bungalows and not others. Ask which way yours faces. Three or four nights is enough for most people; seven can feel long unless rest is the whole point.

paras: The dry season runs from May to October, with lower humidity, cooler nights and a steady trade wind in July and August that can ruffle the lagoons. November to April is warmer, more humid and wetter, with showers that are usually short, lower prices outside the holidays and calm, hot days between the rain. Humpback whales arrive to calve from about August to October and are seen mostly off Moorea.

All international flights land at Papeete, about eight hours from the West Coast of the United States. Flights often arrive in the evening, so plan a first night on Tahiti or on Moorea, at a resort such as {{hotel:Sofitel Kia Ora Moorea Beach Resort}}, before a cruise or an onward flight. The atlas lists {{hotels:country=French Polynesia}} {{page:/hotels/french-polynesia|resorts in French Polynesia}}.

faqs.q: Is a cruise or a resort better for a honeymoon in Tahiti?
faqs.a: A resort, if privacy and rest come first. A cruise, if you would be bored by a week in one place. The best honeymoon here is both: seven nights on a small ship, then three or four in an overwater bungalow on Bora Bora or Taha'a.

faqs.q: How many days do you need in French Polynesia?
faqs.a: At least seven nights after a long flight, and ten to twelve to combine a cruise with a resort stay. With a week, choose two islands at most for a land trip, such as Moorea and Bora Bora, or take a seven-night cruise.

faqs.q: Bora Bora or the Maldives?
faqs.a: The Maldives has more resorts, better house reefs and easier snorkeling from the villa. Bora Bora has mountains, Polynesian culture and other islands to explore, and is closer to North America. For scenery and variety choose French Polynesia; for pure reef and water choose the Maldives.

page.question: Which Hawaiian island is best for a villa stay?
page.title: Which Hawaiian Island Is Best for a Villa Stay? Maui, the Big Island, Kauai and Oahu Compared
page.description: The four main Hawaiian islands compared for a private-home stay: resort-community homes against standalone houses, beaches and swimming by season, driving and flights, and who each suits, across the {{villas:destination=Hawaii}} Hawaii homes in our atlas.
page.capsule: Choose Maui for a first villa stay: good beaches, restaurants and the widest choice of homes near resorts. Choose the Big Island's Kohala Coast for sunshine, golf and homes inside resort communities with club access. Choose Kauai for scenery, hiking and quiet, and Oahu for surf, food and the easiest flights. In winter, pick a south or west shore for calmer swimming.
answer: Each island has its own character, and for a villa the more useful difference is the kind of house you get. In Hawaii there are two sorts. The first is a home inside a resort community, such as Wailea on Maui or Hualalai, Mauna Kea and Mauna Lani on the Big Island, where the house comes with a gate, landscaped grounds and often access to the resort's beach club, pools, golf and restaurants, sometimes for a fee. The second is a standalone house on its own land, more private and more individual, with nobody down the road to bring a towel. Families who want hotel comforts with space should look at the first. Travelers who want to feel they live there should look at the second.

The villa atlas holds {{villas:destination=Hawaii}} {{page:/atlas/villa|Hawaii homes}}: {{villas:destination=Hawaii&location=Oahu}} on Oahu, {{villas:destination=Hawaii&location=The Big Island}} on the Big Island, {{villas:destination=Hawaii&location=Maui}} on Maui and {{villas:destination=Hawaii&location=Kauai}} on Kauai. One point matters before any of the rest. The rules on short-term rentals differ from county to county, are strict in places and keep changing, so the legal standing of a home is a real question in Hawaii. Book a house that is permitted for the stay you are planning, through a company that can show it. A cancelled rental a month before a family trip is the outcome to avoid.

paras: Maui is the safe recommendation for a first stay because it does everything well. Wailea in the south has the calmest beaches and the most polished homes. In the west, the resort areas of Kaanapali and Kapalua are open, while the town of Lahaina is still rebuilding after the 2023 fire, which visitors should approach with some sensitivity.

The Big Island is the least understood. The Kohala Coast is dry lava country with the most reliable sunshine in the state, and its resort communities offer the closest thing in Hawaii to a villa with a five-star hotel attached. The rest of the island, the volcanoes, the rainforest of the Hilo side, the ranch land, is a long drive away and worth a day or two.

sections.h2: Season, swimming and flights
paras: The weather is warm all year, so the season is set by the sea and by school holidays. In winter, large swells arrive from the north. North- and west-facing shores, Kauai's Hanalei, Oahu's North Shore, parts of West Maui, have big surf and are often unsafe for swimming, while south shores stay gentler. In summer the pattern largely reverses and the north shores go calm. For a winter trip with children, choose a south or sheltered west coast: Wailea, Poipu, Kohala or Ko Olina. Kauai's north shore is also much wetter than its south.

The busiest weeks are Christmas and New Year, when homes ask for long minimum stays and book most of a year ahead, then Presidents week, spring break and midsummer. Whale season off Maui runs through the winter months. April, May, September and October are quieter and better value.

All four islands have nonstop flights from the mainland, to Honolulu on Oahu, Kahului on Maui, Kona on the Big Island and Lihue on Kauai, with the widest choice into Honolulu. Flying direct to your island saves half a day against connecting. Two islands in a trip is the sensible limit, with at least five nights on each, and you will want a car everywhere except within a resort.
list: Big family, first time: a resort-community home in Wailea, Maui.
Golfers and grandparents: Hualalai, Mauna Kea or Mauna Lani on the Big Island.
Couples who hike: a house near Hanalei in summer, Poipu in winter.
Surfers and teenagers: Oahu's North Shore in winter to watch, in summer to swim.
A short trip from the West Coast: Oahu, for the flights.

faqs.q: Which Hawaiian island has the best villas?
faqs.a: Maui and the Big Island have the most homes of a high standard near resort services. Maui has more variety and better beaches. The Big Island's Kohala resort communities have the strongest club facilities. Kauai and Oahu have fewer, more individual houses.

faqs.q: Is it legal to rent a vacation home in Hawaii?
faqs.a: Many are legally rented, but the rules vary by county and by neighborhood, are strict in some areas and change from time to time. Book through a company that confirms the home is permitted for short stays, and be cautious of listings that are vague on the point.

faqs.q: Should we stay in a villa or a resort in Hawaii?
faqs.a: A villa suits groups of six or more and stays of a week, when bedrooms, a kitchen and a private pool matter. A resort suits couples, short stays and anyone who wants restaurants and a beach on site. A home inside a resort community gives a good deal of both.

page.question: Grand voyages: what are the 30 to 90 day alternatives to a full world cruise?
page.title: Grand Voyages: The 30 to 90 Day Alternatives to a Full World Cruise
page.description: For travelers who want a long voyage and not four months: grand voyages around one region, back-to-back sailings and long repositioning routes, how they differ from a world cruise segment, who runs them and when, across {{journeys:collection=worldcruise&daysMin=30&daysMax=90}} itineraries of 30 to 90 days in our atlas.
page.capsule: A grand voyage is a single long sailing of about 30 to 90 days around one part of the world: a circle of South America, the Pacific, Africa, Asia or the Mediterranean. It gives you the sea days and community of a world cruise in a third of the time, and at a third of the cost. Seabourn, Cunard, Oceania, Regent, Crystal, Azamara and Holland America all run them.
answer: Most people who say they want a world cruise want some of what it offers: weeks at sea with no flights, a ship that becomes familiar, and a route that goes somewhere difficult. Few can give four or five months to it. The grand voyage is the answer the cruise lines built for them. It is one itinerary, sold as a whole, lasting from a month to about three, and usually devoted to one region so that it goes deeper than a world cruise can: every coast of South America with Antarctica, a circuit of the Pacific from Australia to Japan, Africa from the Mediterranean to the Cape.

Our atlas holds {{journeys:collection=worldcruise&daysMin=30&daysMax=90}} {{page:/journeys/worldcruise|voyages of 30 to 90 days}} alongside the full world cruises: {{journeys:collection=worldcruise&operator=Seabourn&daysMin=30&daysMax=90}} from {{op:worldcruise/Seabourn}}, {{journeys:collection=worldcruise&operator=Cunard&daysMin=30&daysMax=90}} from {{op:worldcruise/Cunard}}, {{journeys:collection=worldcruise&operator=Azamara&daysMin=30&daysMax=90}} from {{op:worldcruise/Azamara}}, {{journeys:collection=worldcruise&operator=Oceania Cruises&daysMin=30&daysMax=90}} from {{op:worldcruise/Oceania Cruises|Oceania}} and {{journeys:collection=worldcruise&operator=Crystal&daysMin=30&daysMax=90}} from {{op:worldcruise/Crystal}}, with more from Princess, Holland America, Regent and Silversea. Some are stand-alone grand voyages and some are long sections of a world cruise, and the difference between those two is worth understanding.

paras: A stand-alone grand voyage and a world cruise segment of the same length feel different on board. On the grand voyage everyone embarks together and the ship plans the whole trip as one: a gala at the start, special shore events, lecturers chosen for the region, and often inclusions such as laundry, a shipboard credit or an overnight tour. On a segment you step into something that began weeks earlier. That can be a pleasure, since the ship is settled and friendly, but the events are aimed at those going all the way round. {{page:/answers/world-cruise-segments-explained|How segments work}} is covered separately.

Back-to-backs are the easiest to arrange and the least special. They are simply consecutive cruises in the same suite. Check that the ports do not repeat, and ask whether the line treats the combination as a single booking for pricing and amenities.

sections.h2: When they sail, and how far ahead to book
paras: Long voyages follow the seasons. From January to April the ships are in the southern hemisphere: South America and Antarctica, Africa, Australia, New Zealand and the South Pacific, which is why so many grand voyages leave in early January alongside the world cruises. Spring and autumn are the seasons for Asia and for the long repositioning routes between regions. Summer belongs to the Mediterranean, Northern Europe, and the Arctic for expedition ships.

They open for sale a year and a half to two years ahead, and the most popular suites go in the first weeks, bought by past guests. Early booking usually brings the best fares and amenities as well as the best choice. Late space does appear, mostly in the smaller suites.
list: Suits: travelers who have enjoyed two or three weeks at sea and want more; the recently retired; anyone curious about a world cruise who wants to test it first.
Suits less well: travelers who want long stays ashore, or who have not yet tried more than a week on a ship.
Choose the region before the line. A circle of South America and a grand Mediterranean are very different trips.
Count the sea days. Pacific and Africa voyages have many; Mediterranean and Asia voyages have few.
Choose the suite with care. Over two months, space and a balcony matter more than on a short cruise.
Insure it. A long voyage is a large, early commitment, with penalties that begin many months out.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a grand voyage and a world cruise?
faqs.a: Length and scope. A world cruise circles the globe, or most of it, in about four to six months. A grand voyage lasts about one to three months and concentrates on one region, such as South America or the Pacific. Both are sold as complete voyages with their own events.

faqs.q: Is a grand voyage cheaper than a world cruise?
faqs.a: In total, yes, because it is shorter. Per day the fares are similar on the same ship and suite, and sometimes a little higher on a grand voyage in a popular region. World cruise guests typically receive the most generous package of inclusions.

faqs.q: Which cruise lines offer grand voyages?
faqs.a: Seabourn, Cunard, Oceania, Regent Seven Seas, Crystal, Azamara, Holland America, Princess and Silversea all sell voyages of 30 to 90 days, under names such as grand voyage or grand adventure. Seabourn also runs long expedition voyages between the Arctic and Antarctica.

page.question: Eastern & Oriental Express: what is it like, and which route?
page.title: Eastern & Oriental Express: What It Is Like on Board, and Which Route to Choose
page.description: Belmond's sleeper train in Southeast Asia explained: round trips from Singapore through Malaysia, the two routes and what each sees, cabins, the open observation car, dining, climate and dress, across {{journeys:vessel=Eastern %26 Oriental Express}} itineraries in our atlas.
page.capsule: The Eastern & Oriental Express is Belmond's sleeper train in Southeast Asia, running three-night round trips from Singapore through Malaysia. Every cabin has a private bathroom, and the open-air observation car is the best seat. Choose Wild Malaysia for jungle and a national park, Essence of Malaysia for Kuala Lumpur, Langkawi and Penang. It is warmer, greener and more relaxed than its European cousin.
answer: The Eastern & Oriental Express is the Asian counterpart of the Venice Simplon-Orient-Express, run by the same company, {{op:train/Belmond Trains|Belmond}}, and quite different to travel on. It began in the 1990s on the line between Singapore and Bangkok, paused in 2020, and returned in 2024 with journeys that stay within Malaysia, starting and ending in Singapore. The carriages are dark green and cream outside, cherrywood and silk inside, and were fitted out for this service, so unlike the European train every cabin has its own shower and toilet. The feature everyone remembers is the open-air observation car at the back, with a bar, where you stand in warm air as rubber plantations, rice fields and jungle slide past.

A journey lasts three nights. You board in the afternoon, dine and sleep on the train, and spend parts of the next two days on excursions before returning to Singapore. On board there are two restaurant cars, a piano bar and a spa carriage. Our atlas holds {{journeys:vessel=Eastern %26 Oriental Express}} {{page:/journeys/train|Eastern & Oriental Express itineraries}}, including packages that add hotel nights in Singapore. There are two routes, usually run in different seasons, so your dates may decide the route for you.

paras: The split follows the monsoon. The east coast of the peninsula is wettest from about November to February, when the train keeps to the west, where Langkawi and Penang are then at their driest. Whichever route you take, the days are hot and humid all year, around thirty degrees, with short heavy showers likely. The train is air-conditioned, and the observation car is not.
Penang is on both routes and is a highlight of each. George Town's shophouses, temples and street food are among the best reasons to come to Malaysia at all.

paras: Meals are a strength. Lunch and dinner are served at tables for two or four in the restaurant cars, with menus that draw on Malay, Chinese and Indian cooking alongside European dishes, and breakfast comes to your cabin. Drinks arrangements vary by fare, so check what yours includes.

Dress is easier than on the Venice Simplon-Orient-Express. Days are smart and light, with comfortable shoes for the excursions. Evenings are cocktail dress or a jacket; black tie is welcome and not required. Pack for heat, and bring a layer for the air conditioning.
list: Compared with the Venice Simplon-Orient-Express: newer carriages, private bathrooms throughout, three nights instead of one, a tropical landscape and a more relaxed mood. Less history, more comfort.
Sleep: the train moves at night on some stretches and the track is old in places. Light sleepers should bring earplugs.
Boarding: the train leaves from Woodlands in the north of Singapore, not the city center, with a transfer arranged from a central hotel.

To extend: fly from Singapore to Langkawi for a beach stay at {{hotel:The Datai Langkawi}}, or on to Bali, Thailand or Vietnam.
Who it suits: travelers who like trains and slow travel, and anyone who has done the European train and wants its opposite. It is not a way to see Malaysia in depth; the stops are short.

faqs.q: Does the Eastern & Oriental Express still go to Bangkok?
faqs.a: Not at present. Since it returned in 2024 the train has run round trips from Singapore through Malaysia. The classic Singapore to Bangkok route is not part of the current program, so check Belmond's schedule if that journey is the one you want.

faqs.q: Do cabins on the Eastern & Oriental Express have private bathrooms?
faqs.a: Yes. Every cabin, including the entry-level Pullman, has its own shower, washbasin and toilet. That is a real difference from the Venice Simplon-Orient-Express, where the original Historic Cabins share facilities.

faqs.q: Which Eastern & Oriental Express route is better?
faqs.a: Essence of Malaysia suits a first visit, with Kuala Lumpur, a day on Langkawi and Penang. Wild Malaysia is the more unusual trip, through rainforest to a national park. They usually run in different seasons, so your travel dates may make the choice.
